l: factual accuracy, Achieving Higher Factual Accuracy in Llama LLM with Weighted Distribution of Retrieval-Augmented Generation
s: Factual accuracy is the reliability of generated information and a central challenge, evaluation target, and primary outcome for large language models. It matters especially in high-stakes environments, real-world deployment, and user trust, where plausible but incorrect outputs are unacceptable. The records begin by identifying factual accuracy as a limitation of Llama’s probabilistic predictions and a broader concern for language models. They describe ways to support it, including fine-tuning, retrieval from external knowledge bases, post-generation fact-checking, and human or metric-based evaluation. The proposed weighted Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach grounds responses in relevant, reliable retrieved information and gives documents weighted influence. Experimental metrics and human evaluations report improved factual accuracy, and the discussion attributes these gains to prioritizing relevant and reliable sources.

l: Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning
s: This February 23, 2024 research article, “Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning,” is by Xingyu Xiong and Mingliang Zheng of the Xiamen Artificial Intelligence Research Institute. It studies whether combining Mixture of Experts (MoE) with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) can improve Large Language Model information retrieval and reasoning. The work uses Mistral 8x7B, an open-source model with a scalable MoE architecture, and evaluates it on Google BIG-Bench. The article begins by identifying shortcomings of Large Language Models in complex retrieval and reasoning: factual errors, outdated knowledge, weak logical deduction, and difficulty using structured knowledge bases. Its related-work discussion presents MoE as a way to distribute work among specialized sub-models through routing, potentially improving efficiency, adaptability, domain performance, and updating. It presents RAG as retrieval plus generation, allowing models to use external, current information and potentially improve factual accuracy, relevance, specialized question answering, and reliability. The methodology integrates both components into Mistral. Query features are extracted, a gating network dynamically routes work and weights specialized expert outputs, relevant documents are retrieved, and retrieved information is incorporated into the generated response. The authors use accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, qualitative assessment, and task-specific measures for evaluation. Implementation includes data preprocessing, iterative training, and efforts to address expert-gating, retrieval, and computational-efficiency challenges. Results show that Mistral+MoE+RAG outperforms both baseline Mistral and Mistral+MoE on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Qualitatively, it produces more detailed, relevant, contextually rich, accurate, and nuanced responses. The discussion frames the combined approach as useful for AI application development and research, improving retrieval, reasoning, contextual richness, and factual accuracy. The article closes by recognizing limits: reliance on Google BIG-Bench and the computational complexity of the integrated model. It proposes future work on scalability, efficient retrieval, and broader language and cultural coverage.

s: “Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning” is a research article and study by Xingyu Xiong and Mingliang Zheng, posted February 23, 2024. It examines integrating Retrieval Augmented Generation and Mixture of Experts into the Mistral 8x7B model to enhance information retrieval and reasoning in complex real-world scenarios. The work evaluates the integrated model quantitatively and qualitatively across varied Google BIG-Bench tasks, aiming to establish the integration’s feasibility and measure its effects. It reports significant improvements in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score, alongside more contextually rich, accurate, and nuanced responses and improved task performance. The article presents the approach as a viable and promising way to overcome traditional LLM limitations, providing empirical evidence for more adaptable, efficient, and intelligent AI systems. It also identifies limits: the scope of the Google BIG-Bench evaluation dataset and the model’s computational demands. The study concludes by calling for validation on broader datasets, community collaboration, and further work on scalability, efficiency, retrieval mechanisms, languages, and cultural contexts, positioning the work as a foundation for future AI research and application.

l: Large Language Models, Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning
s: Large Language Models are deep learning architectures and models with vast parameter counts that demonstrate natural language processing, generation, comprehension, translation, and summarization. They can generate coherent, fluent text, but their most important limitations concern retrieving and processing specific information from vast datasets, integrating and reasoning over it, and handling complex queries needing deep understanding and contextual awareness. They may lack accurate external-source retrieval without explicit training, produce plausible but factually incorrect information, struggle to maintain context and provide accurate references, rely on static training data, and have gaps in deep knowledge, technical expertise, logical deduction, and problem-solving. The study begins by establishing these capabilities and limitations, then examines Retrieval Augmented Generation integrated with a Mixture of Experts architecture as a way to address traditional model limitations. It presents hybrid architectures and possible integration with structured knowledge bases as pathways for improved training and design, concluding that MoE and RAG integration can support future research and applications involving more sophisticated, versatile models.

l: Mixture of Experts, Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning
s: Mixture of Experts is an approach, framework, and advanced methodology in artificial intelligence that diversifies processing capabilities within Large Language Model architectures. It dynamically selects multiple specialized expert models for different data subsets, tasks, or aspects of a query. A gating network routes queries to pertinent experts according to their features, weights their outputs, and aggregates them into a final response. This distribution of computation can improve task-specific performance, adaptability, efficiency, depth, and incremental model updating without comprehensive retraining. In the study, Mixture of Experts is already used by the Mistral 8x7B Large Language Model and is integrated with Retrieval Augmented Generation to improve information processing, retrieval, reasoning, and complex-query handling. The integration supports expert specialization and selection, but requires calibrated gating and adjusted expert-selection thresholds, while adding computational demands. Overall, it supplies specialized expertise alongside Retrieval Augmented Generation and extensive knowledge bases, addressing the trade-off between model generality and specificity and indicating potential for more intelligent, adaptable, and efficient AI systems.

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, Merging Mixture of Experts and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Enhanced Information Retrieval and Reasoning
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation is an advanced artificial-intelligence methodology, paradigm, and mechanism that extends a language model’s access to external information beyond its training dataset. It combines a document retrieval system with a generative model: during generation, a retrieval component searches external knowledge bases or databases for relevant documents, while the generative model incorporates those documents into its response. Documents and queries are projected into a high-dimensional vector space by an embedding function; dense vector searches and normalized similarity scores identify relevant material. The model then generates contextually relevant, factually enriched responses conditioned on retrieved information. Its central value is dynamic access to broad, up-to-date, and specialized knowledge, reported to improve accuracy, relevance, depth, complex question answering, domain-specific performance, reasoning, and task performance, while mitigating biases and inaccuracies. In the reported work, it is integrated into the Mistral 8x7B Large Language Model with Mixture of Experts and evaluated through accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and contextual quality. Implementation requires extracting relevant features and ensuring seamless retrieval and integration; alternative retrieval and integration mechanisms remain a future research direction.

Performance on information retrieval tasks using the Google BIG-Bench dataset is assessed with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. l: Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
s: This unit presents an end-to-end method for answering epidemiological questions about patient health status and healthcare utilization from electronic health records and claims data. It targets databases compliant with the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model and combines large-language-model text-to-SQL generation, medical-entity normalization, and retrieval augmented generation (RAG). Questions are translated into SQL with placeholders for medical entities, which are mapped to precise clinical ontology terms; the resulting coded SQL is executed, and an LLM may optionally formulate an answer from retrieved data. A central contribution is a manually curated dataset of 306 question/SQL pairs, developed with epidemiological-study specialists. Covering 13 tables and 44 columns, it includes complex population selection, temporal relations, aggregation, and mathematical operations. Each pair received two paraphrases, though evaluations used one version per question because of budget limits. Zuzanna Krawczyk-Borysiak created 27 pairs, while A.Z. Jared Worful, Melanie Hackl, and Krawczyk-Borysiak curated the remainder. The evaluation tests GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4 Turbo, GeminiPro 1.0, Claude 2.1, Mixtral 8x7B, and Mixtral Medium on the DE-SynPUF synthetic claims dataset. It compares simple and advanced prompts, RAG, normalization, and SQL execution. Advanced prompts generally improve executability, but relevant retrieved examples provide larger gains, particularly for GPT-4 Turbo and Mistral Medium. GPT-4 Turbo performs best overall; GPT-3.5 Turbo leads in the RAG-top1-oracle setting by closely copying supplied SQL. The unit concludes that RAG is promising and outperforms static prompting, but current models are not reliable enough for unsupervised use. The approach is therefore experimentally deployed at Bayer under monitoring and supervision.

l: OMOP-CDM, Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
s: OMOP-CDM is a common data model that harmonizes observational healthcare data and addresses retrieval variability across databases. Underpinned by standardized vocabularies, it is widely recognized as a standard for RWD analysis and supports conforming claims and electronic health record databases. The released question-SQL pairs dataset adheres to it, enabling applicability across differing RWD data models; conforming databases could provide access to 2.1 billion patient records. It also underlies the OMOP query library, from which fifteen epidemiologically relevant SQL queries were adapted.

l: dataset, Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
s: This is a manually curated, manually annotated dataset for epidemiological research that adheres to the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model. It contains 306 realistic question-SQL pairs spanning 13 tables and 44 columns. Its free-form questions pair with complex SQL involving nesting, multiple logical conditions, aggregation, and mathematical operations; average nesting is 1.5 levels, with 53 samples above two levels and 19 above three. Specialists in epidemiological studies supported its creation. Each pair received two paraphrased question versions, though one version per question was used in subsequent evaluations because of budget limits. It serves as an external knowledge base for RAG by extracting relevant pairs into prompts.

l: Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: This unit presents retrieval augmented response generation (RARG), a system for producing timely, polite, factual counter-responses to online misinformation. It addresses limits of misinformation detection, social correction, and language-generation approaches: user or expert corrections may not scale or include facts, while language models can lack fine-grained knowledge and hallucinate. RARG therefore grounds generation in retrieved scientific evidence. Given a misleading claim, RARG searches a database of more than 1 million academic publications. Its two-stage retrieval pipeline uses BM25 to select a small document subset, then a dense retriever, fden, to rerank evidence. For COVID-19, evidence comes from CORD and LitCovid; the dense retriever is fine-tuned with Check-COVID and additional sampled documents. The retrieved claim-evidence material is passed to fgen, the response generator. Generation begins with supervised fine-tuning, producing an initial and reference model. Human-feedback-based reward models assess refutation, factuality, politeness, claim relevance, and evidence relevance. Reinforcement learning with PPO then updates the actor model, while a KL-divergence penalty keeps it close to the reference model. The resulting actor generates evidence-based responses from the claim and collected documents. Experiments focus on COVID-19 misinformation. The retrieval component outperforms sparse and dense baselines on Check-COVID, and the response component performs strongly on MisinfoCorrect, Constraint, and ANTiVax in both in-domain and cross-domain settings. The RLHF-tuned version generally improves response quality and reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, producing factual, polite, relevant counter-responses. The unit also identifies limits: performance may weaken in domains substantially unlike COVID-19; unreliable evidence can cause inaccurate outputs; and no human evaluation of overall response quality was conducted because of limited scope and budget. Future work aims for a more generalized, domain-adaptive system and improved evaluation.

l: online misinformation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Online misinformation is a growing presence in social-media discussions of trending topics and poses significant threats to the public interest, with delayed intervention associated with outcomes such as vaccine hesitancy. It is detected through content- and evidence-based approaches and commonly countered through social correction; newer language-based methods generate counter-responses or explanations. The records present it as an insufficiently studied setting for retrieval augmented methods. RARG addresses it by retrieving supporting evidence and generating evidence-based responses that explicitly refute inaccurate claims and aim to reduce misinformation’s spread.

l: counter-misinformation responses, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Counter-misinformation responses are produced by users, fact-checkers, and automated methods to prevent misinformation’s continued propagation. Many existing, including social-correction, responses lack politeness, direct refutation, supporting facts, or evidence. RARG is designed to generate polite, factual responses that clearly refute claims, using an actor model based on the input claim and retrieved evidence. During optimization, responses are evaluated for refutation, factuality, politeness, and relevance. Results report improved claim and evidence relevance and stronger quality for in-domain and cross-domain real-world scenarios. However, unreliable evidence sources can introduce inaccuracies and reduce validity.

l: text generation approaches, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Text generation approaches automatically produce counter-misinformation responses; existing end-to-end methods lack external knowledge, leading to subpar text quality and excessively repetitive responses.

l: external knowledge, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_collected_as supporting evidence [for verifying input contents] External knowledge is collected as supporting evidence in evidence-based detection to verify input contents.

l: RARG, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: RARG is an evidence-driven retrieval augmented response generation method and framework for countering online misinformation. It begins by identifying misinformation and collecting supporting evidence from scientific sources through a two-stage evidence-retrieval process. It then uses response generation, including reward estimation and PPO-based fine-grained reinforcement learning, with an actor model after reinforcement learning, to produce evidence-backed counter-responses that are factual, polite, and clearly refute the input misinformation. In experiments on COVID-19, including in-domain and cross-domain settings, its retriever outperforms evaluated baselines, including E5 on top-1 retrieval score and BM25 on Recall@5, while its generator outperforms GPT-3.5 and other baseline generation methods overall and especially in refutation. It performs robustly across contrastive-loss hyperparameter values up to 0.5. Limitations are the lack of human evaluation, possible difficulty in substantially different domains, and unreliable evidence sources.

l: scientific articles, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: RARG collects supporting evidence from scientific sources to inform counter-misinformation responses.

l: retrieval pipeline, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Retrieval pipeline is a two-stage method for response generation that retrieves scientific evidence for an input misinformation claim, then reranks documents. It consists of BM25 and fden; fden scores claim-evidence pairs and also assesses claim-response and evidence-response relevance. Trained to rank annotated pairs highly, it retrieves a relevant subset from a large collection and improves ranking performance on Check-COVID, including with limited subsets.

l: evidence documents, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Evidence documents are scientific articles retrieved and reranked from CORD and LitCovid for response generation. After invalid and duplicate items are filtered, their titles and abstracts form an evidence collection focused on COVID-19. In response to an input claim, top-three or top-five documents are supplied to a generation model to support evidence-based counter-responses, with evidence-response relevance contributing to estimated reward.

l: academic publications, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: has_count over 1M [database size] Academic publications serve as the evidence source for RARG. The authors collected more than 1M academic publications for evidence-based response generation.

l: large language models, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Large language models are language models that embed world knowledge in parameters through extensive pretraining and have achieved substantial improvements in language understanding and generation. They enhance performance across various scenarios, but struggle with fine-grained knowledge and frequently hallucinate because of limited knowledge and reasoning capabilities. In RARG, retrieval-augmented generation incorporates external knowledge and retrieved evidence, while reinforcement learning from human feedback aligns them to produce polite, factual, evidence-based responses.

l: reinforcement learning from human feedback, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Reinforcement learning from human feedback is a method for aligning large language models for evidence-based response generation. After supervised fine-tuning, human-feedback-based reward estimates guide PPO updates to the actor model and tune RARG toward responses of human preference. Its reward design promotes use of retrieved evidence while preserving generated-text quality. In response-generation results, RLHF-tuned RARG improves refutation, factuality, and politeness by an average 2.40% over RARG (S).

l: COVID-19, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: COVID-19 is a case study used to evaluate RARG. Reliable academic research articles related to it define the evidence domain. Across in-domain and cross-domain experiments, RARG outperforms baselines at generating high-quality counter-misinformation responses, while COVID-19 also serves as the reference domain for discussing substantially different test domains.

l: misinformation detection, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Misinformation detection is a language-model-based method for identifying text-based misinformation before counter-responses; it unfolds through content- and evidence-based detection, with images, videos, and propagation paths improving performance.

l: counter-misinformation response generation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Counter-misinformation response generation is a language generation method for early, scalable intervention against online misinformation. Given a misleading claim, it retrieves relevant scientific evidence and generates a polite, factual evidence-based response. RARG frames this as evidence retrieval plus retrieval-augmented response generation, while noting risks from domain shift, unreliable evidence sources, and missing human evaluation.

l: retrieval augmented generation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Retrieval augmented generation is a text generation method that incorporates retrieved, selected external documents as evidence, enabling up-to-date knowledge without expensive retraining. It primarily addresses knowledge-intensive NLP tasks and aims to improve factuality and reduce hallucination. For online misinformation response generation, it remains under-researched; the described work explores evidence-based counter-responses by collecting scientific evidence and performing RLHF alignment.

l: two-stage evidence retrieval, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: RARG evidence collection is a two-stage retrieval pipeline over more than 1M academic articles. It first performs a coarse BM25 search, then uses a fine-tuned dense retriever to rerank retrieved documents, improving relevance estimation, computational efficiency, and retrieval performance when annotated data is limited.

l: response generation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: RARG evidence-based response generation is a component that produces responses to misinformation using collected scientific evidence. It takes an input claim and retrieved evidence documents, included in the prompt, and uses fgen to generate counter-responses. The generation model is first trained end-to-end on MisinfoCorrect, then tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback toward human preferences. Its reward considers evidence use and response quality through refutation, factuality, politeness, claim relevance, and evidence relevance. It is evaluated cross-domain on Constraint and ANTiVax.

l: scientific evidence, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Scientific evidence is collected from relevant documents in a large research corpus for each misleading claim. In retrieval augmented response generation, it serves as supporting material to verify or refute input contents and to generate evidence-based counter-responses that debunk misinformation without retraining the generation model.

l: COVID-19 misinformation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_used_to_validate retrieval augmented response generation [in in-domain and cross-domain experiments] COVID-19 misinformation is the focus of the unit's experiments. RARG is evaluated on both in-domain and cross-domain COVID-19 misinformation and is reported to outperform state-of-the-art methods in generating high-quality responses.

l: evidence-backed counter-response, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: An evidence-backed counter-response is generated after misinformation is identified and relevant evidence is collected. The framework aims for such responses to be polite, factual, and clearly refute the input misinformation.

l: content-based detection, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Content-based detection is a detection approach that trains machine learning models to classify input contents such as claims, incorporating images, videos, and propagation paths to improve performance.

l: input contents, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: A process evaluates an input claim with retrieved evidence to determine the basis for a counter-misinformation response.

l: evidence-based detection, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Evidence-based detection verifies input contents, collecting external knowledge and processing knowledge graphs or retrieved documents to support or refute statements.

l: social correction, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Social correction is a counter-misinformation approach in which users or experts provide comments and replies to curb misinformation, though politeness, evidence, and scale can limit it.

l: language-based methods, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Language-based methods counter misinformation by generating counter-responses and explanations, emphasizing text quality but often neglecting factuality through lack of evidence incorporation.

l: counter-responses, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Counter-responses are generated by RARG using retrieved scientific evidence and RLHF-based alignment. They aim to counter misinformation with factual, polite, relevant, coherent, and effective responses, addressing limits of language-based methods that improve text quality without sufficiently incorporating evidence.

l: explanations, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Language-based methods generate explanations related to misinformation. Existing methods often concentrate on text quality and neglect factuality through evidence incorporation.

l: counter-misinformation response generation framework, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: counter-misinformation response generation framework collects relevant documents, reasons over them, and generates responses in that order.

l: relevant documents, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Relevant documents are collected by the counter-misinformation response generation framework to support the reasoning and generation of responses.

l: REALM, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: REALM is a retrieval augmented method that retrieves Wikipedia documents to solve question answering as conditional generation.

l: fine-grained retrieval, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Fine-grained retrieval has not been well researched for response generation against online misinformation.

l: RLHF-based alignment, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_combined_with fine-grained retrieval [in the research gap identified by the text] RLHF-based alignment has not been well researched in combination with fine-grained retrieval for response generation against online misinformation.

l: fgen, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: fgen is a Llama 2 (7B)-based response generation model and RARG component. It is fine-tuned to generate counter-responses from an input claim and retrieved evidence, then optimized with reinforcement learning; its supervised fine-tuning variant is RARG (S).

l: BM25, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: BM25 is a sparse retrieval algorithm that computes query-document relevance using word frequency in queries and documents. It serves as a baseline and first-stage evidence retriever, efficiently selecting a small subset from a larger collection; RARG uses it in its retrieval module and improves substantially over it.

l: fden, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: fden is a dense retriever in a retrieval module, initialized with E5. It requires large amounts of annotated training data, is fine-tuned on limited claim-evidence pairs to rerank BM25’s subset, combines ranking and InfoNCE losses, and evaluates response relevance to claims and retrieved evidence.

l: sparse retrieval, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_a retrieval approach [used in retrieval augmented generation] It is represented by methods such as BM25, which estimate relevance using word frequency. The text contrasts it with dense retrieval, which provides improved text understanding and relevance estimation.

l: CORD, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: CORD is a database of 1,056,262 COVID-related research articles, used with another database to collect documents, and maintained until June 2022.

l: LitCovid, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: LitCovid is an active collection and database of 301,136 COVID-related research articles, updated through August 2023. It supports collecting articles and supplies sampled documents to enlarge dense retriever training data.

l: Check-COVID dataset, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Check-COVID is a dataset for dense retriever training and evidence-retrieval evaluation. It begins with about 350 evidence documents and 1,000 input-evidence pairs, expands manually to 5,000 CORD and LitCovid documents, and evaluates retrieval using NDCG and Recall at ranks 1, 3, and 5.

l: refutation, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_a response property Refutation is one of the response generation evaluation metrics. RARG achieves the best in-domain score and strong cross-domain scores, while Llama 2 and GPT-3.5 show reduced refutation scores in cross-domain settings.

l: factuality, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Factuality is a response quality targeted during reinforcement learning that evaluates correctness supported by evidence and is used to assess generated responses, where RARG performs strongly in in-domain and cross-domain evaluations.

l: politeness, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Politeness is a response quality and reported generation metric, defined by considerate, thoughtful language that respectfully counters misinformation and avoids backfire. It is targeted during reinforcement learning, with RARG scoring highly and RLHF tuning further improving performance.

l: actor model, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Actor model begins initialized from the supervised fine-tuned reference model, then PPO trains it to improve estimated reward; it generates evidence-based responses for inference.

l: reference model, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: is_a supervised fine-tuned model The reference model is the supervised fine-tuned model used to stabilize reinforcement learning. The actor model is constrained not to deviate significantly from it.

l: reward model, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: A reward model, constructed from human binary feedback, evaluates generated response quality using BERT-based refutation, factuality, and politeness scores, combined with retrieval-based relevance in its estimated reward.

l: Llama 2 (7B), Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Llama 2 (7B) provides the base model for fgen. The resulting RARG system performs similarly to or better than GPT-3.5 on the reported in-domain metrics despite its smaller size.

l: human feedback, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Human feedback is collected as binary labels on response qualities, training smaller reward models through a simpler, more cost-effective preference-ranking approach.

l: supervised fine-tuning, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Supervised fine-tuning teaches a pretrained language model initial counter-misinformation responses, producing a reference model before potentially unstable reinforcement learning for complex tasks.

l: reinforcement learning, Evidence-Driven Retrieval Augmented Response Generation for Online Misinformation
s: Reinforcement learning uses generated responses and reward estimates; proximal policy optimization updates the actor, maximizing expected estimated reward while KL divergence limits deviation.

l: FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: This paper presents NVIDIA’s practitioner-oriented approach to building secure, effective, and cost-efficient enterprise chatbots using large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). It traces enterprise chatbots from fragile dialog-flow systems toward conversational enterprise search enabled by Chat-GPT, vector databases, and RAG, while stressing that enterprise deployments require fresh knowledge, access controls, personal-information protection, and optimization of quality, speed, and cost. The central contribution is the FACTS framework: Freshness, flexible Architectures, Cost economics, Testing, and Security. It is grounded in NVIDIA’s experience with the NVBot platform and three bots: NVInfo Bot, which answers questions over about 500 million enterprise documents while enforcing document permissions; NVHelp Bot, for IT help and HR benefits using about 2,000 multimodal documents; and Scout Bot, for financial earnings using about 4,000 public multimodal documents. The discussion begins with freshness, explaining that frozen foundation models lack enterprise-specific and current knowledge and may hallucinate. RAG addresses this, but retrieval quality depends especially on metadata enrichment, chunking, query rephrasal, and reranking. Hybrid search, agentic architectures, multimodal handling, fine-tuning choices, permissions, evaluation, and ongoing RAGOps monitoring also matter. The paper identifies fifteen RAG pipeline control points. It then describes NVBot’s modular, pluggable architecture, designed to avoid duplicated work in authentication, guardrails, interfaces, monitoring, security, and evaluation. It supports different models, databases, agents, and evaluation frameworks, as well as citizen development, specialized bots, enterprise-wide bots, copilots, and multibot orchestration. On economics, the paper compares large commercial LLMs with smaller and open-source models, finding that smaller models can often offer comparable accuracy with lower cost and latency. It discusses an internal LLM Gateway for auditing, subscriptions, cost control, and vendor-API security, alongside NVHelp Bot evaluations and TensorRT-LLM optimization. Finally, it covers testing and security. Chatbots need security, prompt-change, and regression testing; representative ground-truth data; feedback loops and RLHF; and human oversight because LLM-as-a-judge can reinforce bias. Security requires access control, governance, sensitive-data protection, classification, filtering, and pre- and post-processing controls. NVIDIA adopted Nemo Guardrails because prompt-only guardrails were inconsistent. The paper closes with future work on agentic architectures, enterprise-data summarization, auto-ML optimization, and evaluation of subjective responses and conversations.

l: enterprise chatbots, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Enterprise chatbots are generative AI applications and productivity tools in an enterprise context, intended to enhance employee productivity. They extend company search tools and use enterprise data to answer HR benefits, IT help, sales, engineering, financial earnings, and general enterprise-content questions. Earlier chatbots used dialog flows, intent training, information retrieval, and question answering; newer versions use Large Language Models, Retrieval Augmented Generation, and Langchain/Llamaindex orchestration frameworks for broader conversation. Their successful construction depends on meticulously engineered RAG pipelines and secure, flexible architectures that can support domain-specific, enterprise-wide, and copilot variations. The central challenges are preventing inaccurate or irrelevant responses, maintaining freshness, security, accuracy, and reliability, protecting sensitive data, managing latency and LLM costs, and demonstrating return on investment. Because responses require validation, RAG-based chatbots need lengthy security, regression, automated, ground-truth, and human-oversight testing. Future work targets agentic architectures, updated-data summarization, automated RAG optimization, and stronger evaluation frameworks.

l: generative AI, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots

l: Retrieval Augmented Generation, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Retrieval Augmented Generation is a widely used RAG pipeline component and process in generative-AI-based chatbot construction. It combines retrieval with LLM generation: through semantic matching, it retrieves relevant, fresh enterprise information from vector databases and feeds it to large language models for response generation. Its design unfolds through document retrieval, query rephrasing, reranking, prompting, access controls, references, privacy safeguards, and agent orchestration. Its many control points require careful tuning. What matters most is quality across the FACTS dimensions: freshness, architecture, costs, testing and evaluation, and document security. Approaches discussed for improvement include domain-adapted models, HYDE, FLARE, Self-refine, ReAct, and automated evaluation with RAGAS and ARES.

l: Large Language Models, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Large Language Models are technology and key components of enterprise chatbot systems. They understand user intents from simple natural-language prompts, synthesize enterprise content, and generate coherent, factual, and logical responses. In RAG pipelines, they generate answers from retrieved enterprise information, so quality depends on retrieval relevance and the final prompt. They may be fine-tuned and used in NVIDIA bots, with selectable models in NVInfo Bot and Scout Bot. Large and small models differ in accuracy and latency, while prompt-only guardrails are not followed consistently.

l: NVIDIA, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: NVIDIA is an organization that builds enterprise chatbots to improve employee productivity. It first created three RAG- and LLM-based bots on its in-house NVBot platform: NVHelp Bot for IT and HR benefits, NVInfo Bot for company financial earnings, and Scout Bot for general enterprise content. Its experience showed that successful conversational assistants require careful engineering, execution, evaluation, security, and cost control. Before deployment, it undertook data governance through an enterprise content security initiative, including document-sensitivity classification and excluding sensitive content from chatbots. As use expanded beyond the initial three bots, NVIDIA developed NVBot to avoid duplicated work, engineered RAG pipelines, and implemented an LLM Gateway for payload logging, subscription and API-cost management, and security audits. Its work also informs a FACTS framework and optimization techniques. NVIDIA is now exploring additional domain-specific chatbots, an enterprise-wide chatbot, and copilots as generative AI changes workplace efficiency and information accessibility.

l: FACTS framework, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: The FACTS framework is an evaluation framework for building enterprise-grade RAG-based chatbots. It organizes delivery around five essential dimensions: fresh content, flexible architectures, cost efficiency and LLM cost management, testing, and security. Introduced as a way to deliver chatbots that are fresh, adaptable, cost-efficient, well tested, and secure, it also summarizes challenges and lessons from building three chatbots. It begins with the challenge of keeping enterprise content fresh, then addresses architecture, costs, planning for testing, and security, concluding that these factors are essential to robust enterprise-grade chatbots.

l: RAG pipelines, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: RAG pipelines combine vector-search-based information retrieval systems, Large Language Models, vector databases, and LangChain-like orchestration frameworks. They unfold through metadata enrichment and chunking, document extraction, query rephrasing, retrieval, reranking, prompt design, and response generation, with memory and agents orchestrating activities. Their fifteen critical control points support optimization at each stage. Effective engineering includes semantic-embedding and LLM fine-tuning, access controls, concise responses with pertinent references, and personal-information safeguards. The central concern is improving relevance, accuracy, quality, speed, and cost while managing large- versus small-LLM accuracy-latency tradeoffs; poorly tuned stages can produce hallucinations or irrelevant chatbot responses.

NVIDIA’s chatbot work retrieves and synthesizes such sources; NVInfo Bot addresses about 500 million documents exceeding 7 TB. Because volumes are frequently updated, they are summarized and require freshness management. When commercial LLM vendor APIs are used, data leakage guardrails and an LLM Gateway control access and support audits. Empirical results address accuracy-latency tradeoffs between large and small LLMs.

For complex questions, it added an agent mechanism for query decomposition and orchestration. A fine-tuning experiment with e5-large embeddings showed no significant improvement.

s: Derivative risks in RAG-based chatbots begin with responses lacking original-source context, causing misinterpretation, and expand when enhanced search exposes sensitive enterprise data that is not properly secured.

l: enterprise content security, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: is_a security focus [for internal enterprise chatbots] Enterprise content security is a central focus for the internal enterprise chatbots described in the unit. NVIDIA pursued an initiative for document sensitivity classification and exclusion of sensitive content from chatbots.

l: enterprise documents, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Enterprise documents are protected by access controls, requiring RAG-based chatbots to honor document ACLs during response generation.

l: sensitive data, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Sensitive data can be exposed when enhanced search methods are used with improperly secured enterprise content. The unit describes filtering, classification, guardrails, and content exclusion as measures for protecting it.

l: data governance, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: is_essential safeguarding against unauthorized access and data breaches [before deployment] Data governance should be prioritized before deployment because efficient knowledge access can increase the risk of sensitive data leakage. It is presented as necessary for preventing unauthorized access and data breaches.

l: Nemo Guardrails, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Nemo Guardrails implements enterprise guardrails by processing queries before and responses after use, adopted when LLMs inconsistently followed prompt-expressed guardrails.

l: Our work, FACTS About Building Retrieval Augmented Generation-based Chatbots
s: Our work presents a secure enterprise-grade generative-AI chatbot reference architecture. Building on identified RAG failure points and pain points, it provides 15 control points and solutions across pipeline stages, then addresses complex agentic queries, subjective-response testing, document ACL security, and a flexible chatbot platform.
